# On Small Kindnesses

I've been thinking lately about the asymmetry of kindness—how a moment that costs someone almost nothing can reshape someone else's entire day.

A barista remembering your order. A text that says "thinking of you" unprompted. Someone laughing at your joke even though it wasn't that funny. These tiny gestures seem negligible when you're the giver, but they feel monumental when you're receiving them.

I wonder if we're all walking around starving for small confirmation that we matter, that someone noticed us. We dress it up in bigger language—connection, belonging, love—but sometimes it's just about being seen.

The strange thing is that the people who are best at this rarely know it. They're not performing kindness for credit. They're just genuinely pleased when you succeed, or they instinctively sense when you need a break, or they make space for your weirdness without commentary. It seems effortless from the outside, but I suspect it's actually a form of attention most people don't bother with.

Maybe that's what separates people—not how much they give, but whether they're paying attention in the first place. You can't be kind to someone you haven't really noticed.

So I'm trying to notice more. The colleague who's been quiet lately. The friend I haven't checked on. The stranger who held the door. I'm trying to send the text, give the compliment, remember the detail.

Not because I'm keeping score. But because I know how it feels when someone does, and I'd like to be that person in someone else's story.
